title: Sub-Thermionic Switching in a Negative-Capacitance Bandgap-Change Field-Effect Transistor
authors: Rahul B Awale, Mike Klymenko, Yuefeng Yin, Nikhil V Medhekar, Bhaskaran Muralidharan, Michael S Fuhrer
abstract: Overcoming the approximately 60~mV/dec Boltzmann limit of the subthreshold swing remains a central challenge for low-power nanoelectronics. Negative-capacitance field-effect transistors address it by amplifying the channel potential, but their effectiveness is constrained by capacitance matching and by the quantum capacitance of conventional channels. Here we model a negative-capacitance bandgap-change field-effect transistor (NC-BCFET), in which the ferroelectric gate stack instead amplifies the electric field that opens the bandgap of the channel, using experimentally proven materials: bilayer graphene as a channel with an electrically tunable bandgap and Al$_{0.55}$Sc$_{0.45}$N as the negative-capacitance ferroelectric. Our self-consistent framework couples a four-band tight-binding Hamiltonian with GW-corrected screening, a quasistatic Landau--Devonshire ferroelectric response, and ballistic Landauer--Büttiker transport. Negative capacitance amplifies the interlayer potential difference, compressing the switching window 37-fold relative to a dielectric-gated control. At 300~K, the optimized NC-BCFET achieves a subthreshold swing of 15~mV/dec, four times below the Boltzmann limit, improving to 2.5~mV/dec at 100~K. The room-temperature on/off ratio is limited to $\sim 10^{2}$ by the bandgap of bilayer graphene. The concept extends directly to materials with larger field-tunable bandgaps, where deep subthermionic switching and high on/off ratios can be achieved together at room temperature.
summary: This theoretical work proposes a novel Negative-Capacitance Bandgap-Change FET (NC-BCFET) using bilayer graphene and a ferroelectric gate. By coupling advanced electronic structure calculations with ferroelectric physics, the authors demonstrate that the negative capacitance effect can dramatically reduce the subthreshold swing, achieving values far below the fundamental Boltzmann limit at cryogenic temperatures.
main_problem: The central challenge addressed is overcoming the fundamental 60 mV/dec Boltzmann limit for the subthreshold swing (SS) in low-power nanoelectronics.
main_result: The proposed Negative-Capacitance Bandgap-Change FET (NC-BCFET) achieves an SS of 15 mV/dec at 300 K and an impressive 2.5 mV/dec at 100 K, significantly surpassing the Boltzmann limit.
method: The study employs a self-consistent theoretical framework coupling a four-band tight-binding Hamiltonian with GW-corrected screening and a quasistatic Landau-Devonshire ferroelectric response.
model_or_system: The device utilizes a bilayer graphene (BLG) channel with an electrically tunable bandgap, integrated with an $	ext{Al}_{0.55}	ext{Sc}_{0.45}	ext{N}$ negative-capacitance ferroelectric gate stack.
key_observables: Subthreshold Swing (SS), on/off current ratio ($	ext{I}_{	ext{on}}/	ext{I}_{	ext{off}}$), and the degree of field amplification provided by the negative capacitance effect.
important_parameters: Operating temperatures (300 K and 100 K), ferroelectric thickness ($L_b$), and the bandgap modulation ($\Delta$).
main_assumptions: The model assumes a quasistatic ferroelectric response and uses ballistic Landauer-Büttiker transport theory for current calculation.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the electrostatics of the gated BLG lattice, the band structure showing bandgap opening via an electric field, and potential profiles for different device configurations.
paper_structure: The paper develops the self-consistent model by coupling electronic structure (tight-binding/GW) with ferroelectric electrostatics (L-D theory) and transport (L-B), analyzing performance metrics like SS and on/off ratio across varying temperatures and layer thicknesses.
why_interesting: While focused on solid-state electronics, the core concept of using non-linear, field-dependent material properties (ferroelectrics) to enhance device performance through potential amplification shares conceptual parallels with non-linear dynamics studied in AMO physics.
